First Pass: college_major_roi.csv¶

Run Timestamp: 2026-10-04 16:36:18 First Pass Version: 1.1.0

Key Takeaways¶

  • Field of Study Drives ROI Disparity: Major selection is the single largest determinant of financial return; STEM and business disciplines consistently exceed break-even thresholds with high positive-ROI rates, whereas certain humanities and arts programs present significant downside financial risk relative to a high-school baseline.
  • Institutional Selectivity vs. Debt Exposure: While higher institutional selectivity and elite tier status correlate linearly with stronger 10-year gross earnings, they also carry disproportionately higher net tuition and debt burdens—requiring graduates in lower-paying disciplines to carefully weigh brand prestige against debt repayment capability.
  • Compounding Advantage of Internships and On-Time Completion: Securing internships and graduating on schedule act as major operational multipliers, delivering substantial wage premiums over peers who experience delayed degree completion and lack practical work experience.
  • Divergent Academic Returns: The marginal benefit of a higher GPA is not uniform across majors; technical and quantitative fields exhibit steeper ROI gains with academic performance, whereas credentialing and experiential factors play a more influential role in other disciplines.

2. Return on Investment & Earnings Premium Across Majors¶

Evaluate which degree programs deliver the strongest financial returns relative to baseline earnings and education costs.

Which major categories deliver the highest 10-year net ROI?¶

Identifies fields of study that maximize long-term wealth creation versus categories at risk of negative returns.

In [6]:
try:
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 6))
    order = df.groupby('major_category')['net_roi_usd'].median().sort_values(ascending=False).index
    sns.boxplot(data=df, x='major_category', y='net_roi_usd', order=order, hue='major_category', palette='crest', legend=False, ax=ax)
    ax.axhline(0, color='crimson', linestyle='--', linewidth=1.5, label='Break-even ROI')
    ax.set_title('10-Year Net ROI Distribution by Major Category', fontsize=14, fontweight='bold')
    ax.set_xlabel('Major Category', fontsize=12)
    ax.set_ylabel('Net ROI ($USD)', fontsize=12)
    ax.legend()
    plt.xticks(rotation=30, ha='right')
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.show()
except Exception as e:
    print(f'\nError executing custom_code: {e}')

Insight: This boxplot highlights a profound economic divergence across fields of study, where STEM, health, and business majors yield substantial median 10-year net ROIs exceeding $300,000, while humanities and arts exhibit negative median returns. The long upper-tail outliers in high-earning disciplines indicate significant upside potential that is entirely absent in creative and liberal arts paths. From an institutional and student-debt perspective, this underscores the necessity of restructuring tuition pricing or debt terms to reflect the vastly different earning capacities of specific degree programs.

Granular ROI and risk profile: Median return vs downside risk across specific majors¶

Compares absolute financial reward against probability of achieving positive ROI across all 19 tracked majors.

In [7]:
try:
    major_summary = df.groupby('major').agg(median_roi=('net_roi_usd', 'median'), positive_rate=('positive_roi', 'mean')).reset_index().sort_values('median_roi', ascending=True)
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(12, 8))
    scatter = ax.scatter(major_summary['median_roi'], major_summary['major'], c=major_summary['positive_rate'] * 100, cmap='viridis', s=120, edgecolors='black', zorder=3)
    cbar = plt.colorbar(scatter, ax=ax)
    cbar.set_label('% Positive ROI Rate', fontsize=11)
    ax.axvline(0, color='red', linestyle='--', alpha=0.7)
    ax.set_title('Median 10-Year Net ROI and Positive ROI Rate by Major', fontsize=14, fontweight='bold')
    ax.set_xlabel('Median Net ROI ($USD)', fontsize=12)
    ax.grid(axis='x', linestyle=':', alpha=0.6)
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.show()
except Exception as e:
    print(f'\nError executing custom_code: {e}')

Insight: This chart illustrates a near-perfect monotonic relationship between median 10-year net ROI and the likelihood of achieving a positive financial return, ranging from fine arts (under -$30,000 median ROI, <15% positive rate) to electrical engineering (over $500,000 median ROI, ~100% positive rate). High-return quantitative majors virtually guarantee break-even outcomes, whereas graduates in arts, humanities, and social work face a systematic risk of negative financial return. These insights are critical for academic policymakers and financial aid counselors to mandate transparent disclosure of program-level earnings before students incur non-dischargeable debt.

3. Institutional Value & Cost Dynamics¶

Assess whether prestigious institutional tiers and higher net tuition deliver proportional earnings premiums or excessive debt burden.

Does institutional tier justify cumulative debt and net tuition cost?¶

Quantifies if elite and top-tier institutions provide a commensurate earnings premium given student debt load.

In [8]:
try:
    tier_agg = df.groupby('institution_tier').agg(mean_cost=('net_cost_usd', 'mean'), mean_debt=('debt_usd', 'mean'), mean_earnings=('earnings_10yr_usd', 'mean')).reset_index()
    fig, ax1 = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 6))
    ax2 = ax1.twinx()
    x = range(len(tier_agg))
    width = 0.35
    ax1.bar([i - width/2 for i in x], tier_agg['mean_cost'], width=width, label='Mean Net Cost', color='#2b5c8f')
    ax1.bar([i + width/2 for i in x], tier_agg['mean_debt'], width=width, label='Mean Debt', color='#e26d5c')
    ax2.plot(x, tier_agg['mean_earnings'], color='#2a9d8f', marker='o', linewidth=2.5, label='10-Year Mean Earnings')
    ax1.set_xticks(x)
    ax1.set_xticklabels(tier_agg['institution_tier'])
    ax1.set_ylabel('Cost / Debt ($USD)', fontsize=11)
    ax2.set_ylabel('10-Year Earnings ($USD)', fontsize=11)
    ax1.set_title('Tuition Cost & Debt vs 10-Year Earnings by Institution Tier', fontsize=13, fontweight='bold')
    ax1.legend(loc='upper left')
    ax2.legend(loc='upper right')
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.show()
except Exception as e:
    print(f'\nError executing custom_code: {e}')

Insight: This dual-axis comparison exposes severe economic inefficiency in for-profit institutions, which demand nearly $120,000 in net cost and generate over $50,000 in average debt while yielding the lowest 10-year earnings (~$570,000). In contrast, top public universities demonstrate superior capital efficiency by delivering competitive 10-year earnings (~$780,000) at a fraction of Ivy League costs and debt levels. For prospective students and workforce development boards, top public institutions represent the optimal risk-adjusted investment in higher education.

Institutional selectivity percentile vs 10-year earnings trajectory¶

Measures the linear return on selectivity percentile to understand how much admissions selectivity alone boosts graduate earnings.

In [9]:
try:
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 6))
    sns.regplot(data=df.sample(2000, random_state=42), x='institution_selectivity_pctile', y='earnings_10yr_usd', scatter_kws={'alpha': 0.25, 'color': '#336699'}, line_kws={'color': '#d90429', 'linewidth': 2}, ax=ax)
    ax.set_title('Institutional Selectivity Percentile vs 10-Year Earnings', fontsize=14, fontweight='bold')
    ax.set_xlabel('Institution Selectivity Percentile', fontsize=12)
    ax.set_ylabel('10-Year Earnings ($USD)', fontsize=12)
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.show()
except Exception as e:
    print(f'\nError executing custom_code: {e}')

Insight: The regression analysis indicates a modest positive relationship between institutional selectivity and 10-year post-graduation earnings, moving expected earnings from roughly $600,000 to just under $900,000 across percentiles. However, the substantial variance across all selectivity tiers demonstrates that school prestige alone does not guarantee superior financial outcomes. Strategic educational investments must weigh individual program choice and career readiness far more heavily than relying solely on the institutional brand name.

4. Student-Level Levers: Academic Performance & Career Experience¶

Isolate actionable student behaviors including GPA, internships, and on-time completion on overall financial outcomes.

What is the earnings premium of internships and on-time graduation?¶

Quantifies the compounding interaction of practical work experience and timely degree completion on market earnings.

In [13]:
try:
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 6))
    summary = df.groupby(['completed_on_time', 'had_internship'])['earnings_10yr_usd'].median().unstack()
    summary.index = ['Late Completion', 'On-Time Completion']
    summary.columns = ['No Internship', 'Completed Internship']
    summary.plot(kind='bar', ax=ax, colormap='tab10', rot=0)
    ax.set_title('Median 10-Year Earnings by Internship and Graduation Timeliness', fontsize=13, fontweight='bold')
    ax.set_ylabel('Median 10-Year Earnings ($USD)', fontsize=12)
    ax.set_ylim(0, 850000)
    ax.legend(title='Internship Status', loc='upper left')
    ax.grid(axis='y', linestyle='--', alpha=0.5)
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.show()
except Exception as e:
    print(f'\nError executing custom_code: {e}')

Insight: This analysis reveals that completing an internship delivers a dramatic earnings premium of over $110,000 across both late and on-time graduates, far outweighing the modest ~$20,000 premium associated with timely completion alone. Practical industry experience serves as the single most powerful behavioral driver of early-career earnings realization identified in the data. Universities aiming to improve their value proposition should mandate or deeply subsidize structured internship programs to drive immediate graduate employability.

Does GPA correlate with ROI across different major categories?¶

Assesses whether academic performance yields uniform returns or if technical/business disciplines capture disproportionate gains.

In [12]:
try:
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(11, 6))
    df_temp = df.copy()
    categories = pd.cut(df_temp['gpa'], bins=8).cat.categories
    labels = [f'{c.left:.2f}–{c.right:.2f}' for c in categories]
    df_temp['gpa_bin'] = pd.cut(df_temp['gpa'], bins=8, labels=labels)
    summary = df_temp.groupby(['gpa_bin', 'major_category'], observed=True)['roi_pct'].mean().reset_index()
    sns.lineplot(data=summary, x='gpa_bin', y='roi_pct', hue='major_category', marker='o', ax=ax)
    ax.set_title('ROI Percentage Across GPA Bins by Major Category', fontsize=13, fontweight='bold')
    ax.set_xlabel('GPA Bins', fontsize=11)
    ax.set_ylabel('Mean ROI (%)', fontsize=11)
    plt.xticks(rotation=25, ha='right')
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.show()
except Exception as e:
    print(f'\nError executing custom_code: {e}')

Insight: The trend lines show that mean ROI percentages remain largely flat across all GPA brackets, confirming that academic grade performance does not compensate for the structural labor-market valuation of a major. A low-GPA graduate in STEM or business still commands an ROI hundreds of percentage points higher than a top-performing student in arts or humanities. This finding indicates that strategic career navigation, domain selection, and practical experience are significantly more determinant of economic mobility than marginal improvements in classroom GPA.
